> **What this case shows** — a clinical ADL scale records *that* a person can
> groom or eat (capacity); a wrist accelerometer can record whether they actually
> **do** it (the ICF **performance** qualifier). Under a strict
> leave-one-subject-out test on real single-wrist data, the ecosystem's
> activity-recognition pipeline separates self-care from getting around well
> (**0.94** of self-care windows land on *some* self-care activity) and
> recognises **grooming** (brushing/combing, ICF d520, recall **0.77**) and
> **drinking** (d560, **0.81**) cross-subject. **What reproduces, and what
> doesn't** — grooming and drinking reproduce; **eating (d550) does not** (recall
> **0.00**): eating-from-a-plate collapses into the other hand-to-face gestures,
> so a wrist alone cannot name it. This is the honest boundary of wrist-only
> self-care recognition, reported rather than averaged away. **How to read it** —
> left, cross-subject recall per activity (red = self-care, dashed = 0.20
> chance); right, the ICF performance profile of the recognised self-care time.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — turn raw wrist acceleration into an ICF performance profile in
four moves: **window** the signal → **extract** activity-recognition features →
**classify** each window → **map** the activities to ICF codes.
**Way of thinking** — validate the honest question, *can these be told apart on a
real wrist, across people?*, and answer it at the level the sensor supports:
self-care vs locomotion first, then which tasks within. Test on held-out subjects
(same-subject accuracy flatters), and when a class fails, name it — a 0.00 recall
is a finding, not a failure to hide.
**Ecosystem usage** — chain one function per role: `adlFeatures()` →
`trainADL()` / `recognizeADL()` → `adlToICF()` (PhysioWearable); the classifier is
swappable for a stronger PhysioML model without changing the recipe.
:::

## Proposition

Under leave-one-subject-out on real wrist accelerometer data, the HAR pipeline
separates self-care from locomotion (self-care-as-self-care **0.94**) and
recognises **grooming (d520, 0.77)** and **drinking (d560, 0.81)** cross-subject,
but **eating (d550) is not distinguished (recall 0.00)** — it collapses into the
other hand-to-face gestures. Five-class accuracy is **0.60**.

## Question & goal

**The question comes from the dataset's own design.** The HMP dataset (Bruno et
al. 2014) was built to test *activity-of-daily-living recognition from a single
wrist accelerometer* — the placement of a smartwatch. It recorded real self-care
tasks (brushing teeth, combing hair, eating meat and soup, drinking from a glass)
alongside walking and stair-climbing, so recognition methods could be scored
against ground-truth labels. We ask the dataset's question and add the clinical
one: do the recognised activities map to the ICF codes that make them a
*performance* measure?

## Challenge & approach

Self-care ADLs are hard on the wrist because several are the *same broad motion* —
a hand travelling to and from the face. The approach does not pretend otherwise.
We window the acceleration, extract a compact 36-feature descriptor per window
(per-axis and vector-magnitude statistics, signal-magnitude area, dominant
frequency, spectral entropy, jerk), train a dependency-free k-nearest-neighbours
classifier, and test **leave-one-subject-out** — every subject held out once.
`adlToICF()` then maps each recognised activity to its ICF performance code.

## Data

The **HMP** wrist-worn accelerometer ADL dataset (Bruno et al. 2014, UCI #283) —
a single tri-axial wrist accelerometer at 32 Hz, 13 subjects. The exact activity
folders used are recorded in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Cross-subject recall per activity (left; red = self-care, dashed = 0.20
chance) and the ICF performance profile of the recognised self-care time
(right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* on the left, each bar is one activity's recall under
leave-one-subject-out — grooming and drinking clear the chance line, **eating sits
at zero**, and the stair contrast is weak. On the right, the recognised self-care
time as ICF d-codes — the *performance* side of the capacity–performance picture,
dominated by the two tasks the wrist can actually resolve.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| self-care detected as self-care (leave-one-subject-out) | **0.94** |
| grooming (d520) recall / drinking (d560) recall | 0.77 / 0.81 |
| **eating (d550) recall** | **0.00** (not distinguished) |
| 5-class cross-subject accuracy | 0.60 |
| subjects | 13 |

## Conclusion

A wrist accelerometer reliably tells **self-care from getting around**, and can
name **grooming and drinking** — but it **cannot name eating** from the wrist
alone; the hand-to-mouth motion is indistinguishable from the other hand-to-face
gestures. The transferable takeaway: **recognise at the level your sensor
supports, map what resolves to ICF performance, and state the class that fails
(eating here) as a finding — the honest boundary is part of the result.**

## Open questions

- Eating collapses into the other hand-to-face gestures under a wrist-only sensor
  (recall 0.00); whether a richer feature set, a stronger model, or an added
  finger/utensil sensor separates it — and whether dressing/toileting are
  recognisable from the wrist at all — is open. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

The recipe is general to any wearable ADL-recognition task.

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| window + extract HAR features | `adlFeatures()` | PhysioWearable |
| train / apply an activity recogniser | `trainADL()` / `recognizeADL()` | PhysioWearable |
| time budget per activity | `adlBudget()` | PhysioWearable |
| map activities to ICF performance codes | `adlToICF()` | PhysioWearable |

They chain through per-window feature rows. **Choosing the parameters:** match
the window to the activity timescale (2.56 s here); recognise at the granularity
your sensor supports (self-care *category*, then the tasks that resolve); always
split by subject and report the classes that fail. Swap the k-NN for a stronger
model (PhysioML `rocket()`) when you have labels — the ICF mapping is unchanged.

```r
library(PhysioWearable)
feats <- adlFeatures(accel, sampling_rate = 32)     # windowed HAR features
model <- trainADL(train_feats, train_labels)
recog <- recognizeADL(model, accel, sampling_rate = 32)
adlToICF(recog)                                     # -> ICF performance profile
```

Apply it to your own hypothesis by recording the activities you care about and
retraining; pair it with the capacity side (`adl-rasch-verbagg`) to quantify the
capacity–performance gap.
